claims.claim: The technology industry has been hollowing out the meaning of ownership for years.
Firmware updates are the incremental mechanism by which this hollowing out occurs.

sentences.reason: Both halves make descriptive assertions about real-world industry behavior and a specific technical mechanism over time; a reader can reasonably ask 'how do you know that?' for each. Neither is supplied by the request.

Sets up a conditional definition: if a maker can disable features post-sale, the arrangement resembles a lease. It draws an inference from a stated condition rather than asserting a free-standing external fact.
Extends the definitional argument from p1s2, characterising the purchase as a conditional license. No new external descriptive fact is introduced.
Rhetorical invitation to recall a conceptual state of affairs before software-enabled devices; functions as framing for the argument that follows, not an assertion about the external world.
States a definitional account of what a sale is. The claim is analytic/definitional rather than a report on external legal practice or doctrine.
Clearly imagined scenario (dealer sending a signal to disable heated seats, launching a subscription tier) used to illustrate the argument; not reported as a real event.

claims.claim: Manufacturers desire or would prefer to disable hardware features and monetise them as subscriptions.

sentences.reason: The parenthetical 'we all know they'd love to' asserts a real-world fact about manufacturer intentions/motivations as a known current reality, not a hypothetical. A reader can ask 'how do you know that?'

claims.claim: Device makers have been building into products the architecture of post-sale remote feature modification for roughly a decade.
Such modifications are delivered invisibly via patches that download while users sleep.
Public outrage over this practice has not kept pace with its actual prevalence.

sentences.reason: Three distinct descriptive claims about industry practice over time, the technical delivery mechanism, and comparative public response — none supplied by the request and all independently checkable.
Transitional sentence framing what follows; no independent factual assertion.
Generic illustrative setup ('you pay full retail, take the thing home') functioning as a hypothetical/argumentative premise rather than a report about a specific real event.

claims.claim: Companies have reclassified previously included device features as premium add-ons and removed them via silent software updates after purchase.

sentences.reason: Describes real industry conduct as a general practice, not a hypothetical; a reader can ask 'when and where has this happened?'

claims.claim: Manufacturers disclose feature changes in changelogs written in legalistic language not intended to be read by ordinary users.

sentences.reason: 'Change-log written for lawyers, not users' asserts a real common practice about how manufacturers communicate changes; it is a descriptive industry-practice claim, not pure reasoning.
Rhetorical question prompting the reader to apply a concept; no independent factual assertion.
Asserts what the reader 'would call' the scenario and what action they 'would want'; a value judgment about appropriate labelling and response, not a report on what courts or regulators currently do.

claims.claim: Society and legal institutions currently treat post-sale software feature removal as a terms-of-service matter rather than a property matter.
The technology industry has an interest in maintaining this framing and has worked toward it.

sentences.reason: Both halves make descriptive claims about real-world legal/social treatment and industry strategic interests; neither is supplied by the request and a reader can fairly ask 'how do you know that?'

claims.claim: John Deere has taken the position that its tractor software is licensed rather than sold, giving the company ongoing control over customer use of the hardware.

sentences.reason: Named-company factual claim about a real legal/commercial position not supplied by the request; requires independent verification.

claims.claim: Tesla remotely modified battery range on vehicles that customers had already purchased.

sentences.reason: Named-company factual claim about a specific real-world action not supplied by the request; requires independent verification.

Summarises the structural argument being made (physical transfer vs. retained functional control); no new external fact introduced.
Characterises the EULA defense as 'genuinely dishonest' — a framing move that sets up the argument, not a new external descriptive claim.

claims.claim: EULAs typically bury relevant clauses deep in lengthy boilerplate text presented in small or discouraging type.

sentences.reason: 'Buried past forty screens of boilerplate, in type sized for discouragement rather than reading' asserts a real common industry practice about EULA formatting; a reader can ask whether this is actually the case.
Rhetorical question drawing an inference from the premise in p5s2; no new external fact.

Hedged personal assessment ('I don't think this is hard to fix, in principle'); framing for the proposals that follow, not an external claim.
Policy recommendation only; no claim about what current law or practice actually is.

claims.claim: Existing right-to-repair statutes carve out or otherwise fail to cover the software layer of devices.
The software layer is where manufacturers' actual control over device functionality resides.

sentences.reason: The normative demand ('we need… statutes with real teeth') embeds two descriptive claims: the current state of right-to-repair law and where device control actually lives. Per the system prompt, a normative sentence that also asserts facts about current law or institutions is not purely normative.

claims.claim: Courts currently treat lengthy boilerplate EULA agreements as sufficient evidence of informed consent.

sentences.reason: The normative demand ('we need courts to stop treating…') presupposes and asserts a current reality about how courts treat boilerplate agreements. Per the system prompt, mixing 'should' with a claim about what courts currently do is not purely normative.
Pure value assertion that the word 'sale' ought to carry meaning; no external descriptive fact claimed.

claims.claim: Sellers of software-governed devices do not genuinely intend to honor the implicit promise of full ownership conveyed by a purchase transaction.

sentences.reason: 'Every buy button is a promise the seller never intends to keep' is a descriptive assertion about real seller intentions at scale, not a pure normative statement. A reader can ask 'how do you know sellers don't intend to keep it?'
